case_study_insert.main_stem: Yarrow Hempcrete Works (YHC) is a cooperative in the eco-insulation building materials sector, employing a workforce of 54. Founded in 2012 by Aisha Yarrow, it makes carbon-negative hempcrete blocks for green builders and operates a democratic leadership structure. YHC plans to invest $880,000 in a hemp-processing and block-pressing line using a carbon-negative lime binder, financed by a $350,000 bank loan, a $280,000 share issue and $250,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $330,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $15.50, and currently produces 75,000 units a year. YHC faces two problems: crack defects average 4.2% and hemp shiv waste is 5.2%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report, 2025: the new hempcrete block line produced 19,000 blocks with a crack-defect rate of 2.6%, down from 4.2% on the old line. Customer complaints about insulation performance fell from 28 to 13 per month. Delivery lead time averages 5 days. A survey of 380 green builders found that 59% would specify hempcrete and 52% would pay up to $0.70 more per block for carbon-negative certification. Hemp shiv waste is 5.2% on the old process against 2.4% on the new. Logs show 13 of 54 members trained on the new press; external courses cost $700 each.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Yarrow Hempcrete Works for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base rate rose from 4.0% to 4.9%, increasing borrowing costs. (2) The minimum wage increased 6.4% from $12.80 to $13.62 an hour from April 2026. (3) Hemp shiv and lime input costs rose 9.8% year-on-year; construction inflation is 6.0% and green-material sales grew 3.9%.

questions.question_text: YHC financed $280,000 of its $880,000 expansion through a share issue. Explain two advantages for YHC of a share issue over a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue raises $280,000 without interest or capital repayments, so YHC can invest in the carbon-negative lime binder line while already carrying fixed costs of $330,000 a year and a $350,000 bank loan. Dividends need only be paid if profits allow, which suits a cooperative still trying to cut crack defects from 4.2% toward 2.6%.

Point 2: Equity does not require collateral, so the $880,000 pressing line is not exposed to repossession if green-material sales slow to 3.9%, and the balance sheet is strengthened for future borrowing. The share issue also lets YHC keep its $250,000 retained profit for the 5-day delivery cycle and to absorb the 9.8% rise in hemp shiv and lime costs, rather than committing every source of cash to debt service.

Equity also suits a cooperative, since members share in the upside of the $880,000 line, and keeping the $350,000 loan as the only debt limits interest exposure while the 4.2% crack-defect rate is reduced.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to YHC's share issue, loan and costs.

questions.question_text: YHC is launching its carbon-negative hempcrete blocks. Consider national television advertising, eco-building trade shows, or influencer and social media campaigns. Which should YHC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television: TV would give hempcrete blocks mass awareness quickly, which could help a cooperative reach beyond its regional base. But the buyers are the 380 green builders in YHC's survey, not the general public, so most exposure is wasted. For a business funding an $880,000 pressing line, TV is expensive and cannot communicate the carbon-negative certification that 52% of builders value.

Eco-building trade shows: These bring YHC face to face with the 380 surveyed green builders, of whom 59% would specify hempcrete and 52% would pay $0.70 more for certification. Staff can show the 2.6% crack-defect rate and 2.4% pilot waste, explain the lime binder and take orders. Costs are contained relative to the investment, though the audience is narrower and success depends on stand quality and follow-up.

Influencer and social media: Eco influencers can tell the carbon-negative story cheaply and quickly, supporting the 52% premium signal and reaching younger builders. However, the audience is broad and often not the specifiers who buy blocks, so engagement may not convert into the 75,000-unit volume, especially given the 5-day delivery lead time that favours committed local customers.

Recommendation: YHC should choose eco-building trade shows. They target the exact 380 builders, demonstrate the certification that 52% demand and convert the 59% specification interest into orders at controlled cost. Television is rejected as expensive and untargeted, and influencers are rejected as awareness without a buying channel; YHC should use cheap social content to reinforce the trade-show message.

With a 5-day delivery promise, the local relationships built at trade shows are worth more than distant awareness, because repeat orders from the 380 builders depend on reliable supply of the blocks.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with little YHC context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options applied to YHC's green-builder market.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why television and influencers are rejected.

questions.question_text: YHC is a cooperative with democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for YHC of this approach in reducing the 5.2% hemp shiv waste.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the workforce of 54 a voice in how the pressing line is run, so members can suggest practical ways to cut the 5.2% hemp shiv waste and share in the 2.4% pilot performance. Involvement raises ownership of waste-reduction routines, which helps YHC move crack defects from 4.2% toward the 2.6% achieved on the new line.

Point 2: As a cooperative, open discussion fits the ownership structure and keeps all members committed to the $880,000 investment, since they are also owners. Better ideas from the 13 already trained on the press can be spread quickly through flat communication, protecting the $15.50 selling price and $8.00 variable cost from scrap losses while the carbon-negative lime binder beds in.

Because members are also owners, the 2.4% pilot waste becomes a shared goal rather than a management instruction, which supports the $880,000 investment and the 5-day delivery commitment. This also helps retain trained members on the press.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to YHC's waste, ownership and defects.

questions.question_text: YHC must train 13 of its 54 members on the new press. Consider on-the-job training or external courses at $700 each. Which should YHC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the press suits YHC's own hempcrete and lime-binder process, costs no course fees and keeps all 13 members productive, protecting output of 75,000 blocks. Trainers can pass on the settings that achieved the 2.6% crack-defect rate immediately. The drawbacks are that no formal certificate is awarded, even though 52% of surveyed builders pay more for carbon-negative certification, and that a senior operator loses time coaching others.

External courses: Courses at $700 each for 13 members cost 13 × $700 = $9,100, modest against the $880,000 line, and give a recognised qualification that strengthens the carbon-negative claim to the 380 surveyed builders. Outside expertise could also reduce the 5.2% shiv waste. However, 13 of 54 members are off the press during training, reducing capacity, and a generic course may not match YHC's exact mix, so on-site follow-up is still needed.

Decision: YHC should choose external courses for the 13 members. The carbon-negative certification that 52% of builders pay for needs a credible, recognised credential, making the $9,100 and short loss of capacity worthwhile, and outside input can tackle the 5.2% waste. On-the-job training is rejected as the main route because it cannot provide that certificate and risks embedding the habits behind the 4.2% crack defects; YHC should add brief on-site coaching to cover plant-specific settings.

Paying $9,100 is small beside the $880,000 line, and the short absence of 13 of 54 members is offset by the credibility needed to sell carbon-negative blocks to the 380 surveyed builders.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with little YHC application.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods applied to YHC's 13 members and costs.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and uses the $9,100 computation.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how YHC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $330,000 ÷ ($15.50 − $8.00) = $330,000 ÷ $7.50 = 44,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 44,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $15.50 − $8.00 = $7.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways YHC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 44,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 75,000 units to show a margin of safety of 31,000 units, indicating how far green-builder orders can fall before the $880,000 line stops covering costs.
2. Use the $7.50 contribution per unit to test the $0.70 certification premium: accepting it lifts contribution to $8.20, so managers can judge whether a small discount still covers the $330,000 fixed costs.
3. Check financing capacity: at 75,000 units YHC is well above break-even, so managers can test whether the $350,000 bank loan remains serviceable if green-material sales growth slows to 3.9%.
4. Monitor unit cost of $12.40 ($330,000 ÷ 75,000 units + $8.00) each quarter; a rise would signal the 5.2% shiv waste is increasing scrap cost and prompt action on the press.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 44,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 31,000-unit margin of safety vs 75,000 output; $0.70 premium modelling against $330,000 fixed costs; servicing the $350,000 loan; and $12.40 unit-cost benchmarking to track 5.2% waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate YHC's profitability. Has YHC's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 38.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 42.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 14.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.5%
ROCE 2025 = 17.5%

Detailed workings: Revenue rose from $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 and cost of sales from $620,000 to $696,000, lifting gross profit from $380,000 to $504,000. Operating profit grew from $100,000 to $168,000 while capital employed increased from $800,000 to $960,000; interest payable was $12,000 then $16,000.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. Gross margin rose from 38.0% to 42.0%, reflecting better control of hemp and lime use as shiv waste falls from 5.2% toward 2.4%. Operating margin improved from 10.0% to 14.0% because operating profit grew much faster than revenue, evidence of fixed-cost leverage as output approaches 75,000 blocks. Returns on capital increased from 12.5% to 17.5%, so the $880,000 pressing line is adding profit per dollar employed despite the new debt and equity. The caution is that construction inflation of 6.0% and green-material sales growth of only 3.9% could limit orders, making the higher fixed base a risk if demand softens.

Conclusion: YHC's profitability has improved: gross margin, operating margin and ROCE all rose together, so the investment is paying off. To protect the 42.0% gross margin and 17.5% return, YHC should secure long-term hemp shiv and lime supply and convert the 59% specification interest into firm builder contracts.

Operating profit rose by $68,000 while revenue rose by $200,000, so cost control as well as volume is lifting returns; with only $16,000 of interest, the 17.5% return on the $960,000 capital base is a solid result.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States figures with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates margins and returns for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of revenue, costs and capital and a justified conclusion on whether profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for YHC of producing carbon-negative hempcrete blocks.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Carbon-negative hempcrete matches a clear market signal: 59% of the 380 surveyed green builders would specify it and 52% would pay $0.70 more for certification, helping YHC protect its $7.50 contribution per unit while hemp shiv and lime costs rise 9.8%. The pilot's 2.4% waste and 2.6% crack-defect rate also suggest lower scrap and a stronger green brand for a cooperative.

Disadvantage: The carbon-negative lime binder and certification are costly, which can lift the $8.00 variable cost per unit and require the full $0.70 premium across all 75,000 blocks to protect margins. Inconsistent hemp shiv supply could push crack defects back toward 4.2% and raise waste above 5.2%, increasing costs and delaying the 5-day delivery promise to builders.

YHC must convert the 52% premium interest among the 380 surveyed builders into real orders, or the extra binder and certification cost cannot be recovered and the $330,000 fixed costs weigh on each of the 75,000 blocks.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using YHC's survey, costs and defect data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base rate rise to 4.9%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in hemp shiv and lime costs will affect YHC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.9%): If YHC's $350,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.9 percentage points cost 0.9% × $350,000 = $3,150 a year (0.009 × $350,000). That is modest against fixed costs of $330,000 and can be removed by fixing the rate. Dearer credit could also slow the green-material sales that grew only 3.9%, a secondary demand effect.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.62 an hour): With a workforce of 54, some pressing and packing hours are hourly paid, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours or pay rates, so an annual wage total would be invented; the defensible comparison is productivity of 75,000 units ÷ 54 staff, about 1,389 units per worker. If that holds, the $7.50 contribution can absorb the rise; if output falls, unit labour cost increases.

Hemp shiv and lime costs (9.8%): These are core inputs to every block. Since the $8.00 variable cost is not decomposed, only a labelled bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 9.8%, that adds 9.8% × $8.00 = $0.78 a unit (about $0.784), or roughly 75,000 × $0.784 = $58,800 a year. Even a partial pass-through reduces the $7.50 contribution that must cover $330,000 fixed costs and service the $880,000 line, though the $0.70 certification premium recovers part of it.

Conclusion: The 9.8% rise in hemp shiv and lime costs has the greatest impact. It applies to every block, directly erodes the contribution that justifies the investment, and cannot be removed by fixing an interest rate. The interest rise is small and fixable, and the wage rise can be absorbed while productivity stays near 1,389 units per worker, so both are secondary.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited YHC application.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on YHC's costs or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
